{{Short description|American chemist (1921–2014)}}
'''James N. Pitts Jr.'''  (January 10, 1921&nbsp;– June 19, 2014) was an [[Americans|American]] [[chemist]] and researcher known for his work in the fields of [[photochemistry]] and [[atmospheric chemistry]]. Pitts was a pioneer in the study of [[smog]] and [[air pollution]], especially in [[Los Angeles County]].<ref name=ocregister>{{cite news|first=Raymond |last=Mendoza |title=Obituary: James Pitts, 93, pioneer in air pollution research |url=http://www.ocregister.com/articles/pitts-624311-air-chemistry.html |work=[[Orange County Register]] |date=2014-06-19 |access-date=2014-07-18}}</ref><ref name=ucirvine>{{cite news|first=Janet |last=Wilson |title=Pollution expert James Pitts dies, 1921-2014  |url=http://www.universityofcalifornia.edu/news/pollution-expert-james-pitts-dies |work=[[University of California, Irvine]] |date=2014-06-19 |access-date=2014-07-18}}</ref> Pitts co-founded the Statewide Air Pollution Research Center at the [[University of California, Riverside]] in 1961 and served as the center's director from 1970 to 1988.<ref name=latimes>{{cite news|first=Tony |last=Barboza |title=James Pitts dies at 93; his research led to cleaner air in California  |url=http://www.latimes.com/local/obituaries/la-me-james-pitts-20140626-story.html |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=2014-06-25 |access-date=2014-07-18}}</ref> He authored more than 400 scientific publications and four books on the subjects, especially smog.<ref name=latimes/>

Pitts' research formed the basis for [[California]]'s [[air quality]] laws.<ref name=latimes/> According to the chair of the Air Resources Board, Mary Nichols, "Jim Pitts was probably the single person most responsible for the understanding of what strategies we need to clean up [[Southern California]]'s air...He was able to explain all of this in English to policymakers so that they would be able to accept that it was going to take extensive and difficult actions to control [[Air pollution|emissions]]."<ref name=latimes/> He often invited state and federal officials to his smog chamber at UC Irvine, including [[Jerry Brown]] and [[Ronald Reagan]], to demonstrate the effects of smog and air pollution.<ref name=latimes/> In a common demonstration, Pitts would fill an [[Erlenmeyer flask]] with [[ozone]] and then twist a slice of [[lemon]] onto the flask. The ensuing chemical reaction, which quickly produced a fog, demonstrated the formation of smog in the [[atmosphere]].<ref name=latimes/>

Pitts refused funding from industry groups, which increased his center's credibility.<ref name=latimes/> He was the recipient of numerous awards and recognitions from the [[California State Assembly]], the [[United States Congress]], the [[Coalition for Clean Air]], the South Coast Air Quality Management District, and the California state air board.<ref name=ocregister/>

Pitts was born on January 10, 1921, in [[Salt Lake City]], [[Utah]], to Esther (''[[née]]'' Bengtson) and James N. Pitts.<ref name=ucirvine/> The family moved to [[West Los Angeles]] when he was just six months old.<ref name=latimes/> A high school teacher sparked his interest in chemistry during his junior year.

Pitts enrolled as a chemistry student at [[University of California, Los Angeles]] (UCLA) in 1939.<ref name=latimes/> He left during [[World War II]], joining a group of young scientists who conducted classified [[chemical warfare]] field tests.<ref name=latimes/> Their work led to the development of more effective gas mask for Allied forces during the war.<ref name=latimes/> He returned to UCLA, where he received a [[bachelor's degree]] in [[chemistry]] in 1945 and a doctorate in 1949.<ref name=latimes/> Pitts initially worked as a faculty member of [[Northwestern University]]. He was at the time married to a woman by the name of Nancy Ann Quirt. James and Nancy had three daughters Linda, Christie and Beckie.

Pitts was hired as a founding professor at [[UC Riverside]] in 1954.<ref name=latimes/>

Pitts married his second wife, [[UC Irvine]] chemist and professor [[Barbara J. Finlayson-Pitts|Barbara Finlayson-Pitts]] in 1970.<ref name=latimes/> He followed her to the University of California, Irvine in 1994, where the two collaborated of research and co-authored books and other publications.<ref name=latimes/>

James Pitts died of natural causes at his home in [[Irvine, California]], on June 19, 2014, at the age of 93. He was survived by his wife, Barbara Finlayson-Pitts, and three daughters,  Linda Lee, Christie Hoffman and Beckie St. George.<ref name=latimes/> He was also survived by five grandchildren Kristin Cohn, Brianna Hoffman, Trevin Hoffman, Mallory St George and Ryan Giordano. His great-grandchildren include Brandon, Kyle, Austin and Riley.
